text: The 2013 El Reno tornado was an extremely large, powerful, and erratic tornado that occurred on the early evening of Friday, May 31, 2013, in a rural area of Central Oklahoma. It was a rain-wrapped, multiple-vortex tornado that peaked at a record width of 2.6 miles (4.2 km), making it the widest tornado ever recorded. The tornado formed at 6:03 p.m. CDT (23:03 UTC), about 8.3 miles (13.4 km) west-southwest of El Reno, and rapidly grew in size and intensity as it tracked through central Canadian County. It remained over mostly open terrain and did not impact many structures, but mobile weather radar measurements revealed extreme wind speeds exceeding 313 mph (504 km/h), among the highest ever observed on Earth, just slightly below the 321 mph (517 km/h) recorded during the 1999 Bridge Creek–Moore tornado. The tornado reached its maximum width of 2.6 miles as it crossed U.S. 81, surpassing the previous record set in 2004, and then turned northeastward, weakening before dissipating around 6:43 p.m. CDT (23:43 UTC) after tracking 16.2 miles (26.1 km). It avoided densely populated areas near the Oklahoma City metropolitan area. The tornado killed four storm chasers—three professional and one amateur—marking the first known deaths in storm chasing history. These chasers, including TWISTEX scientists and engineers Tim Samaras, Paul Samaras, and Carl Young, were caught off-guard by the tornado’s immense size and erratic movement. Paul Samaras and Young were ejected from their Chevrolet Cobalt by a sub-vortex, while Tim remained buckled in the passenger seat. Local resident Richard Henderson, who took a photo of the tornado before being struck, also died. Other chasers, such as Mike Bettes of The Weather Channel and Reed Timmer, were injured or had their vehicles damaged. A Doppler on Wheels analysis revealed that all teams were hit by an intense internal sub-vortex with winds approaching 200 mph (320 km/h), moving in a complex pattern. The tornado was responsible for eight fatalities and 151 injuries. Due to its size, ferocity, irregular movement, and the storm chaser deaths, it became one of the most studied and infamous tornadoes, with the National Weather Service calling it "the most dangerous tornado in storm observing history." The tornado developed within a larger weather system involving a mid-to-upper level trough and a closed mid-level low pressure area moving east-northeastward, with a strong polar jet over the southern Great Plains. Dewpoints ranged from the upper 60s°F (20°C) to lower 70s°F (20–22°C), temperatures were in the low to mid-80s°F (27–30°C), and CAPE values ranged from 3500 to 5000 J/kg, with deep layer wind shear of 45–55 kn (52–63 mph), creating favorable conditions for severe storms. A Particularly Dangerous Situation Tornado Watch was issued at 3:30 p.m. CDT, and a tornado warning was issued at 5:33 p.m. CDT for Canadian County. The tornado initially formed as multiple sub-vortices, deviated from its path at 6:15 p.m. CDT, looped before resuming east-southeast motion, and killed two people at 6:23 p.m. CDT as it passed south of El Reno across U.S. 81. It then moved into more populated areas of Canadian County, prompting a tornado emergency, before turning northeast and passing over Interstate 40 at 6:42 p.m. CDT, killing two more people. The tornado was on the ground for 40 minutes along a 16.2-mile (26.1 km) path. A strong anticyclonic multi-vortex satellite tornado formed southeast of the primary tornado at 6:28 p.m. CDT and remained on the ground for 15 minutes before lifting at 6:43 p.m. CDT. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) initially rated the tornado EF3 based on damage, but later upgraded it to an EF5 rating based on mobile radar data, with wind speeds preliminarily estimated at over 296 mph (476 km/h), and a revised analysis in 2015 showing peak winds of 313 mph (504 km/h). A 2024 NOAA and University of Oklahoma analysis estimated wind speeds between 115–150 m/s (257–336 mph; 414–540 km/h). Despite the radar-measured wind speeds, NOAA revised the rating to EF3 in August 2013 because ground damage surveys did not support a higher rating, citing the rural nature of the area and the fact that the EF5 wind speeds occurred in sub-vortices that did not impact structures. The tornado’s unusual behavior included abrupt direction changes, rapid expansion to 2.6 miles in about 30 seconds, a swift increase in forward speed from 20 to 55 mph (32 to 89 km/h), multiple vortices, and a translucent outer circulation obscured by rain. This made it a worst-case scenario for storm chasers, with many located in the "bear's cage" area northeast of the tornado, where visibility was good but reaction time was minimal. The wrapping rain bands were part of the tornado’s outer circulation, not a narrow corridor of clear air. Tim Samaras, Paul Samaras, and Carl Young were among the first known tornado-related deaths of professional storm chasers or researchers. Tim drove a reinforced truck, while Carl drove an unmodified Chevrolet Cobalt, which was underpowered and poorly suited for high winds and rain-slicked roads. Mike Bettes had his SUV thrown 200 yards, suffering a broken neck and fractured vertebrae, while Emily Sutton and Kevin Josefy had their vehicle damaged by debris. Billy Prater and his family sought refuge under an overpass, Brandon Sullivan and Brett Wright were struck by barn debris, and Reed Timmer’s vehicle lost its hood. Dan Robinson escaped just ahead of the TWISTEX crew and is believed to be the last person to see Samaras, Paul, and Young. A tour group led by Randy Walton and Mike Phelps escaped after turning around as the tornado approached. A Doppler on Wheels analysis showed that all vehicles entered the tornado through the less intense north/northwestern side and were then hit by the intense internal sub-vortex. In response to the deaths, Kansas Emergency Management Association president Brian Stone called for storm chasing regulations, though implementation remains uncertain. AccuWeather Senior Vice President Mike Smith urged against overreacting, noting that the chasers were the first to die in 40 years and that storm chasing provides vital real-time data. On June 2, dozens of storm chasers coordinated a tribute using GPS transponders to spell out the initials of Tim, Paul, and Carl in North Dakota, South Dakota, and Nebraska. The Discovery Channel aired a special tribute episode titled "Mile Wide Tornado: Oklahoma Disaster" on June 5, honoring the chasers and covering the May 20 Moore tornado. The November 2013 National Geographic cover story featured Tim Samaras and a detailed scientific analysis of the tornado. A team of scientists and veteran chasers launched a crowd-sourcing project to collect video, photos, and GPS logs to reconstruct the event, creating the largest visual data set ever gathered on a tornado. The data is combined with radar and lightning information and aims to develop a standardized open-access database. In 2015, software called "Tornado Environment Display" (TED), named after Dr. Ted Fujita, was unveiled to synchronize maps, radar data, and storm chaser footage.

A documentary titled *Mile Wide Tornado: Oklahoma Disaster* was released on June 5, honoring three storm chasers and covering the events of the EF5-rated tornado that struck Moore and parts of southern Oklahoma City eleven days earlier, on May 20. The November 2013 issue of *National Geographic* featured a tribute to Tim Samaras, a National Geographic Explorer supported in part by the Society, and included a detailed scientific analysis of the tornado. A team of scientists and veteran chasers conducted a crowd-sourcing survey to collect storm chaser data, such as video, photographs, and GPS logs, creating the largest visual dataset ever assembled on a tornado. This information was combined with radar and lightning data, and the project aims to develop a standardized open-access database for future events. In 2015, software called "Tornado Environment Display" (TED), named after Dr. Ted Fujita, was unveiled to synchronize maps, radar data, and storm chaser footage; Anton Seimon, one of its architects, noted that while it had been used only in relation to the El Reno tornado, it could be applied to future tornadoes with sufficient footage. The tornado moved over mostly open terrain, resulting in relatively light damage—though still significant in isolated areas—according to National Weather Service surveys, with structures sustaining at most EF3-level damage. The Oklahoma City West Livestock Market was described as a "war zone," with several large steel-frame warehouse buildings destroyed, multiple large brick buildings at the Canadian Valley Technology Center heavily damaged or destroyed, and a large metal wind turbine prop blade thrown 100 yards (91 m) into a daycare building, with damage at that site estimated at up to $40 million. One farmstead, including a large barn, cattle barn, three machine sheds, granaries, and the owner’s home, was completely destroyed. Several rural homes were destroyed, large amounts of gravel were blown off roads leaving only dirt exposed, and multiple large metal electrical transmission poles, trees, and vehicles were damaged or tossed. At least 29 buildings and 40 vehicles were damaged or destroyed, with repairs in the El Reno area expected to take at least a year. On June 1, the American Red Cross established a shelter at Redlands Community College in El Reno for storm victims. The following day, Oklahoma Governor Mary Fallin visited damaged areas of El Reno. A state of emergency was already in effect due to the May 20 tornadoes, enabling residents to quickly access emergency aid. Homeless residents were provided temporary housing in shipping containers, each equipped with a kitchen, bedroom, living room, and bathroom. Eight people died in the tornado, all in vehicles. Local hospitals, including OU Medical Center, INTEGRIS Southwest Medical Center, and Mercy Hospital in El Reno, reported at least 115 injured, including five critical patients, with a total of 151 injuries attributed to the event. As the tornadoes approached the Oklahoma City metro, thousands of residents evacuated, possibly due to memories of the May 20 EF5 tornado’s devastation, causing Interstates 35, 40, 44, and 240 to become "parking lots" with chaotic traffic, including people traveling southbound in northbound lanes. It has been suggested that the evacuation was partially driven by a controversial on-air recommendation from KFOR-TV chief meteorologist Mike Morgan, who advised residents without underground shelters to evacuate south of the tornado’s path, contrary to the recommended safety plan of seeking an interior room, bathtub, or closet without windows. Dr. Jeff Masters of Weather Underground stated that if the tornado had tracked directly over one of the congested highways, the death toll could have easily exceeded 500. The tornado’s location was 35°28′45″N 97°54′00″W (35.4792°N 97.9°W).
